en: The Buddha Spoke the Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Rice Seedling.

Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as various bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Together.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra went to the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya was walking to and fro; having arrived, they exchanged greetings and sat together upon a flat stone.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya in this way: "Maitreya!
Today the Blessed One, having observed a rice seedling, spoke thus to the bhikṣus:..."
“O bhikṣus! If one sees dependent origination, one sees the Dharma;
if one sees the Dharma, one is able to see the Buddha.”
Having spoken these words, he remained silent and said nothing more. Maitreya,
for what reason did the Sugata speak thus?
What are these matters?
What are their causes and conditions?
And what is the Dharma?
Who is the Buddha? How is it that by seeing dependent origination one is able to see the Dharma?
And how is it that by seeing the Dharma one is able to see the Buddha?
Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya replied to the Venerable Śāriputra:
“Now the Buddha, the Dharma King, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has told the bhikṣus:
‘If one perceives dependent origination, one is able to perceive the Dharma;’”
Regarding the statement, "If one sees the Dharma, one is able to see the Buddha," what herein constitutes the causal condition (*nidāna*)?
As for the causal condition, it is this: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises.

That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. In this way, there is only the arising of this entire mass of pure suffering.

In this context, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair cease. Thus, there is the cessation of this entire mass of pure and extreme suffering.
This is the Dharma of dependent origination taught by the Blessed One.
What is this Dharma? It is the eightfold noble path:
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—
this is the Noble Eightfold Path, as well as its fruit and Nirvana.
That which the World-Honored One has taught is called the Dharma. "Who is the Buddha?

One who is said to know all dharmas is called a Buddha, because by means of that eye of wisdom and the Dharma-body, he is able to see and realize bodhi, as well as the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training."
"What is the vision of dependent origination?

It is as the Buddha has taught: if one can see the dharma of dependent origination as being permanent, devoid of a life-principle (*jīva*), free from a life-principle, the nature of reality (*yathābhūtatā*), non-erroneous, unarisen, unoriginated, uncreated, unconditioned, unobstructed, without objective domain, quiescent, fearless, unassailable, and characterized by non-quiescence—this is it."

If one can thus perceive phenomena as permanent, devoid of life, free from vitality, characterized by suchness, non-erroneousness, non-arising, non-origination, non-action, unconditioned, unobstructed, objectless, tranquil, fearless, unassailable, and lacking the mark of non-tranquility—then, by attaining right knowledge, one is able to awaken to the supreme Dharma and perceive the Buddha through the unsurpassed Dharmakāya.
Question: "For what reason is it called 'causes and conditions' (hetu-pratyaya)? Answer:

"To have a cause and to have a condition is what is called 'causal condition' (*hetu-pratyaya*); it is not because of being without cause or without condition that it is so named; therefore, it is called the phenomenon of causal conditions.
The Blessed One has briefly explained the characteristic of causal conditions: those conditions produce a fruit."

Whether a Tathāgata appears or does not appear, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains eternally present. Thus it is said regarding the nature of phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the fixedness of phenomena, the nature of being in accordance with causes and conditions, suchness, non-erroneousness, immutability, reality, the limit of reality, non-falsity, and non-perversion.
This dependent origination arises by means of two kinds.
What are these two? They are the correspondence of causes and the correspondence of conditions.
That [dependent origination] is further twofold: namely, external and internal.
Among these, what is the external dependent origination associated with causes?

It is as follows: from the seed arises the sprout; from the sprout arises the leaf; from the leaf arises the stalk; from the stalk arises the node; from the node arises the ear; from the ear arises the flower; and from the flower arises the fruit.
If there is no seed, the sprout will not arise;
likewise, if there is no flower, the fruit will not arise.
When there is a seed, the sprout arises.
In this way, when there is a flower, the fruit also arises.
That seed does not form the thought:
"I am able to produce the sprout."
The sprout, too, does not form this thought:
"I am produced from the seed.
This continues up to the flower, which likewise does not form such a thought.
"The fruit thinks, 'I can produce the fruit,' yet the fruit itself does not have this thought:
'I am produced from the flower.'"
"Nevertheless, because there is a seed, the sprout is able to arise;
likewise, because there is a flower, the fruit is thereby able to be accomplished.
One should contemplate the meaning of the correspondence of causes in external dependent origination in this way."
"How should one contemplate the meaning of the conditional correspondence of external dependent origination?
It is said to be due to the conjunction of the six elements.
By what six elements is there conjunction?"
That which is called the combination of the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and time arises through external dependent origination.
One should contemplate the meaning of the correspondence of conditions in external dependent origination in this way.
The earth element is able to support the seed;
the water element moistens and saturates the seed;
the fire element is able to warm the seed.
The wind element causes the seed to move;
the space element does not obstruct the seed;
and time is able to transform the seed.
If these various conditions are absent, the seed will be unable to produce a sprout.

However, if the external earth element is not lacking, and likewise water, fire, wind, space, and time are all present without deficiency, then through their total conjunction, when the seed ceases, the sprout is able to arise. In this process, the earth element does not form the thought:
"I am able to support the seed."
In this way, the water element does not form the thought:
"I am able to moisten the seed.
The fire element also does not form the thought:
"The fire element does not form this thought: 'I am able to warm the seed.
Nor does the wind element form this thought:
'I am able to cause the seed to move.'"
The space element also does not form this thought:
"I am able to provide no obstruction to the seed.
Nor does the season form this thought: [“I am able to provide no obstruction to the seed.”]
"I am able to transform the seed," nor does the seed itself think,
"I am able to produce the sprout."
The sprout, too, does not form this thought:
"I am now produced from these various conditions.
Nevertheless, when these conditions exist, the sprout arises at the very moment the seed ceases; likewise, when there is the flower, the fruit arises.

That sprout is not produced by itself, nor is it produced by another, nor is it produced by both itself and another; it is not produced by Īśvara, nor does it arise through the transformation of time, nor is it born from self-nature, nor does it arise without a cause.
Nevertheless, when the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and time come together, the sprout arises at the moment the seed ceases.
Therefore, one should contemplate the principle of the correspondence of conditions in external dependent origination in this manner.
"One should contemplate those external dependent origination phenomena through five aspects.
What are these five? They are:
not eternal, not annihilated, not transmigrating, producing great results from small causes, and being similar to those [causes]."
Why is it not eternal?
Because the sprout and the seed are each distinct from one another.
That sprout is not the seed; the sprout does not arise at the time the seed perishes.
Nor does it arise without ceasing.
When the seed perishes, the sprout arises; therefore, it is not eternal.
How is it not discontinuous?
The sprout does not arise from a past seed that has already perished, nor does it arise without the seed having ceased;
rather, while the seed is perishing, the sprout arises like the simultaneous rising and falling of the ends of a balance scale. Therefore, there is no interruption.
How is it that there is no transference?
The sprout is distinct from the seed;
since the sprout is not the seed, there is therefore no transference.
How does a great fruit arise from a small cause?
From a small seed a great fruit arises; therefore, a great fruit arises from a small cause.
In what way is it similar to that [seed]?
Because the fruit produced corresponds to the seed that was planted, it resembles that [seed].
Thus, one contemplates the external conditions of dependent origination through five aspects.
"In this same way, the internal conditions of dependent origination also arise by means of two kinds."
What are the two? They are the correspondence of causes and the correspondence of conditions.
What is the meaning of the correspondence of causes regarding the internal dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
This refers to beginning from ignorance as the condition for volitional formations, up to birth as the condition for old age and death.
If ignorance does not arise, volitional formations do not exist;
likewise, if birth does not exist, old age and death do not exist.
Thus, because there is ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise;
and so on, until because there is birth (*jāti*), aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) come to be.
Furthermore, ignorance does not form the thought:
"I am able to produce volitional formations.
Nor do the volitional formations form this thought:
"I have arisen from ignorance."
"Even birth does not form this thought:
'I am able to produce old age and death.
Nor does old age and death form this thought:"
"I have come from birth.
Nevertheless, it is because of ignorance that volitional formations arise; likewise, because there is birth, aging and death come to be.
Therefore, one should contemplate the meaning of the causal correspondence of the internal dependent origination in this way.
How should one contemplate the matter of the conditional correspondence of the internal dependent origination?
It is through the conjunction of the six elements.
By what six elements (*dhātu*) is there a conjunction?
It is through the conjunction of the so-called earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
In this way, one should contemplate the phenomena associated with conditions within the internal law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
What is the characteristic of the earth element within the internal dependent origination?
That which provides solidity and hardness to this body is called the earth element.
That which causes this body to cohere is called the water element.
That which can digest what the body eats, drinks, chews, and consumes is called the fire element (*tejodhātu*).
That which acts as the internal and external inhalation and exhalation within this body is called the wind element (*vāyudhātu*).
That which creates vacuity and penetration within this body is called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).

The five bodies of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) in association with their objects, as well as the outflow-tainted mental consciousness (*sāsravamanovijñāna*), which—like bundles of reeds—are able to bring about the sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) of this body, is called the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*).
If these various conditions do not exist, the body will not arise.

If the internal earth element is not incomplete, and likewise, if the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements are all complete without exception, then through their total integration, the body is born.
The earth element also does not form this thought:
"I am able to perform the function of solidity within the body.
The water element also does not form this thought:
"I am able to effect the accumulation for the body.
The fire element also does not form the thought:
"I am able to digest the food, drink, chewing, and eating of the body."
The wind element also does not form the thought:
"I am able to produce the internal and external inhalation and exhalation.
The space element also does not form the thought:
"I am able to perform the function of creating internal voidness within the body.
The consciousness element (vijñānadhātu) likewise does not form the thought:
"I am able to bring to fruition this sprout of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) within the body."
The body, likewise, does not form this thought:
"I am produced from these various conditions.
Nevertheless, when these various conditions exist, the body is produced.

That earth element is also not the self, not a sentient being, not a life-principle, not a living soul, not a human youth, not an agent, not male, not female, not a eunuch, not autonomous, not "mine," nor is it any other such thing.

In this way, even the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element are not the self, not a sentient being, not a life-principle, not a living being, not a youth, not an agent, not male, not female, not neuter, not autonomous, not "mine," nor anything else.

What is ignorance? Regarding these six elements, to give rise to the notion of oneness, the notion of a composite, the notion of permanence, the notion of solidity, the notion of indestructibility, the notion of bliss, as well as the notions of a sentient being, a life-force, a living soul, a nourisher, a spirit, a person, a human, a youth, an agent, a self, and what belongs to a self, along with other various forms of non-knowing—this is ignorance.
Because there is ignorance, one gives rise to greed, hatred, and delusion toward various objects.
This giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion toward various objects is "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise";
that which is able to discern these various phenomena is called "consciousness."
The four aggregates of clinging that arise together with consciousness are "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa);
the sense faculties based upon name-and-form are called the "six sense bases" (ṣaḍāyatana);
the conjunction of these three factors is called "contact" (sparśa).
The experiencing of contact is called feeling (*vedanā*);
attachment to feeling is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
the intensification of craving is called grasping (*upādāna*).
The karma that arises from grasping and is capable of producing future existence is called "becoming" (bhava);
the aggregates produced from that cause are called "birth" (jāti);
and once born, the maturation of those aggregates is called "aging" (jarā).
The aging of the aggregates and their dissolution is called death;
at the time of death, possessing internal attachment and feverish distress is called sorrow (*śoka*);
the utterances that arise from sorrow are called lamentation (*parideva*).
That which is experienced as suffering by the five consciousnesses and the body is called *duḥkha* (suffering);
that which is experienced as various sufferings by the mental faculty (*manas*) through volitional attention is called *daurmanasya* (grief);
and that which is accompanied by these and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) is called *upāyāsa* (despair).
Because it is a great darkness, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*);
because it performs formative activity, it is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);
because it discerns, it is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because they depend on one another, they are called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);
because they serve as gateways for birth, they are called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*);
and because of contact, they are called contact (*sparśa*).
Because of experiencing, it is called sensation;
because of thirsting, it is called craving;
because of grasping, it is called clinging.
Because it exists after birth, it is called "existence" (bhava);
because it produces the aggregates (skandhas), it is called "birth" (jāti);
because the aggregates mature, it is called "aging" (jarā).
The disintegration of the aggregates is called death;
sorrow is called grief;
lamentation is called wailing.
Because it afflicts the body, it is called suffering (*duḥkha*);
because it afflicts the mind, it is called grief (*daurmanasya*);
because it is a mental affliction, it is called vexation (*upāyāsa*).
Furthermore, the failure to comprehend true nature and the presence of inverted ignorance is called *avidyā* (ignorance).
Because there is thus *avidyā*, it is able to bring about the three types of formations (*saṃskāra*), namely: meritorious formations, non-meritorious formations, and immovable formations.
That from meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*) arises consciousness of meritorious formations is "conditioned by ignorance are formations" (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*);
that from non-meritorious formations arises consciousness of non-meritorious formations is called "conditioned by formations is consciousness" (*saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam*);
and that from immovable formations arises consciousness of immovable formations is called "conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form" (*vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam*).
Because name-and-form (nāmarūpa) increases, that which is able to perform functions through the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) is "name-and-form as condition for the six sense bases.
That which arises from the six sense bases as the sixfold collection of contact (sparśa) is "the six sense bases as condition for contact.
That which arises from the object of contact as sensation (vedanā) is called "contact as condition for sensation."
Having discerned feeling (*vedanā*), the arising of defiled craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and attachment is called "craving conditioned by feeling.

Because one knows [the object] and gives rise to defiled craving and attachment, not wishing to distance oneself from pleasant forms and well-being, but instead giving rise to longing and desire—this is "clinging conditioned by craving.
Having given rise to longing and desire, the performance of karma leading to future existence through body, speech, and mind—this is "existence conditioned by clinging."
The aggregates produced from that karma are "existence-conditioned birth";
once born, the maturation and disintegration of those aggregates is what is called "birth-conditioned aging-and-death."

Therefore, these twelve factors of dependent origination act as causes for one another and as conditions for one another; they are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither causeless nor conditionless, neither subject to grasping, nor subject to exhaustion, nor subject to destruction, nor subject to cessation.
Since beginningless time, it has continued like a torrential stream without interruption.

Nevertheless, these twelve links of dependent origination act as causes for one another and as conditions for one another; they are neither permanent nor impermanent, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither causeless nor conditionless, neither subject to grasping, nor subject to exhaustion, nor subject to decay, nor subject to cessation. Since beginningless time, they have continued like a torrential stream without interruption.
“There are four branches that can encompass the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination.
What are these four? They are namely:
ignorance, craving, karma, and consciousness.”
Consciousness takes the nature of seeds as its cause;
karma takes the nature of a field as its cause;
and ignorance and craving take the nature of afflictions as their causes.

In this context, karma and the afflictions are able to produce the consciousness that serves as the seed; karma acts as the field for the seed-consciousness, craving moistens the seed-consciousness, and ignorance plants the seed-consciousness.
If these various conditions are absent, the seed-consciousness cannot be established.
That karma, too, does not form the thought:
"I am now able to act as the field for the seed-consciousness."
Craving also does not form the thought:
"I am now able to moisten the seed-consciousness.
Ignorance also does not form the thought:
"I am now able to plant the seed-consciousness.
That seed-consciousness also does not form the thought:
"I am now arising from these various conditions."

Nevertheless, the seed-consciousness, depending upon that field of karma and moistened by craving, produced in the soil of ignorance and entering the mother’s womb, is able to give rise to the sprout of name-and-form.

That sprout of name-and-form is not created by itself, nor is it created by another, nor is it created by both self and other together; it is not a transformation of Īśvara, nor is it altered by time, nor does it arise from intrinsic nature, nor is it produced by a creator, nor does it arise without cause.
Although at the time of the union of the parents and the convergence of other conditions, the dharma of selflessness is devoid of self and what belongs to a self, being just like empty space.

Because those illusory phenomena possess all necessary causes and conditions without exception, they enter the mother’s womb based on their place of birth and are thereby able to accomplish the consciousness that grasps and maintains the seeds.
"The sprout of name-and-form is like the arising of visual consciousness: it arises when five conditions are present. What are these five?
They are the basis, the eye, visible forms, light, and space."
Based on attention (*manasikāra*), visual consciousness arises.
In this process, the eye serves as the basis (*āśraya*) for visual consciousness,
while visible form (*rūpa*) serves as its object (*viṣaya*).
Luminosity can perform the function of manifestation;
emptiness can perform the function of non-obstruction;
and mental attention can perform the function of conceptualization.
If these various conditions are absent, visual consciousness does not arise.

If the internal sense-base of the eye is not deficient, and likewise, if form, light, space, and attention are all present without deficiency, then when all these factors come together, visual consciousness arises.
That eye also does not form this thought:
"I am now able to serve as the basis for visual consciousness.
Nor does the visible form think:
"Light does not form the thought: 'I am now able to perform the function of manifesting for visual consciousness.'"
Space also does not form the thought:
"I am now able to perform the function of non-obstruction for visual consciousness.
Mental attention likewise does not form the thought:
"I am now that which is perceived by visual consciousness," yet that visual consciousness also does not form the thought:
"I exist because of these various conditions."
"Nevertheless, with these various conditions, visual consciousness arises.
This should be understood accordingly for the other sense faculties as well.
Thus, not even the slightest dharma moves from this world to another world."
Nevertheless, because causes and conditions are all fully present, the fruits of karma also manifest.
It is like the reflection of a face appearing within a clear mirror.
Although the reflection of the face does not move into the mirror, because the causes and various conditions are fully present, the reflection of the face nevertheless appears.
In the same way, although not even the slightest thing passes from here to another place, because the causes and various conditions are fully present, the fruit of karma nevertheless appears.
For example, the lunar disc travels forty-two thousand yojanas from here.
When the reflection of that lunar disc appears in a small vessel containing water, the lunar disc itself does not move from its original place to that vessel of water.
Nevertheless, because causes and conditions are all fully present, the lunar disk also appears.
In this same way, although not even the slightest thing passes from here to another place, because causes and conditions are all fully present, the fruit of karma also appears.
For example, just as fire cannot burn if its causes and conditions are not complete,
but can indeed burn when its causes and conditions are fully present.
Thus, these phenomena are without self and devoid of "mine," being like empty space.

Relying upon those illusory phenomena, because causes and conditions are fully assembled, when entering a mother’s womb at the place of birth, one is able to accomplish the seed-consciousness and the sprout of name-and-form produced by karma and afflictions.
Therefore, one should contemplate the phenomena associated with conditions within the internal law of dependent origination in this way.
"One should contemplate the internal law of dependent origination through five aspects. What are these five?"
It is neither eternal, nor discontinuous, nor transferred; from a small cause a great fruit arises, yet it is similar to that [cause].
How is it not eternal?

That is to say, those final aggregates at death and those aggregates at birth are distinct; because the final aggregates at death are not the aggregates at birth, and because the final aggregates at death have ceased while the aggregates at birth have appeared, it is therefore not eternal.
What is meant by "not being annihilated"?
It is not that the factors of rebirth (upapatti-bhava) obtain at the time when the final aggregates (cyuti-skandha) perish;

nor is it that they do not perish, for those final aggregates also perish. At that very moment, the aggregates of rebirth arise like the rising and falling of a scale's ends; therefore, there is no annihilation.
Why is there no transmigration?
Because sentient beings are able to arise from a state that lacks a commonality of group (*asabhāga*) into a state that possesses a commonality of group (*sabhāga*), there is no transmigration.
Why is it that a great fruit arises from a small cause?
By performing even a minor action, one experiences a great maturation; therefore, a great fruit arises from a small cause.
Because the performed cause brings about that fruit, it is similar to it.
Therefore, one should contemplate the dharma of dependent origination through five aspects. "Venerable Śāriputra!

If there is anyone who, by means of right wisdom, constantly contemplates the dharma of dependent origination as taught by the Tathāgata—seeing it as being without a life-principle (*jīva*), free from a life-principle, of suchness, non-erroneous, unarisen, unproduced, uncreated, unconditioned, unobstructed, without objective domain, quiescent, fearless, unassailable, inexhaustible, characterized by non-quiescence, non-existent, empty, deceptive, lacking solidity, like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow, a fault, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—[that person shall attain liberation]."
Did I exist in the past, or did I not exist?
One does not discriminate regarding the limits of the past.
One does not discriminate regarding the future limit, such as thinking, "Where will I be born in a future age? What is this? And how is this?"
What kind of beings are they?
From where have these sentient beings come?
Having ceased to exist here, where will they be born?
Nor does one discriminate regarding the existence of the present.

Furthermore, one is able to extinguish the various divergent views held by the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world, namely: the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, the view of a person, the view of rarity, the view of auspiciousness, and the views of opening and closing.
Because of thorough understanding,
just as a tāla tree is completely cut down at its root, one clearly severs the sprouts of the sense-faculties and realizes in future lives the dharma that is neither born nor extinguished.
“Venerable Śāriputra!

If there is anyone who is fully endowed with such patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and is well able to discern this law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān will immediately bestow upon them the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”

When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya had spoken these words, Śāriputra and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others—hearing the Dharma taught by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Rice Seedling Spoken by the Buddha.
